Is the City Councillor for Scarborough-Guildwood and Deputy Mayor of Scarborough, I am proud to serve the residents of our community and champion the interests of Scarborough across Toronto. Throughout more than 20 years of elected public service, I have remained focused on delivering results, strengthening neighbourhoods, and ensuring Scarborough has a strong and respected voice at City Hall.

I believe effective leadership is built on collaboration. As Deputy Mayor, I have worked closely with municipal, provincial, and federal partners to advance priorities that matter most to residents, including housing, transportation, community safety, infrastructure, economic development, and social services. My goal has always been to ensure Scarborough receives its fair share of resources, investment, and opportunity.

Residents deserve representation that is accessible, accountable, and focused on practical solutions. Through regular conversations in our neighbourhoods, on the TTC and GO Transit, at community events, places of worship, and monthly Town Hall meetings, I hear directly from the people I serve. What I hear consistently is that residents want leaders who listen, work together, and solve problems.

Throughout my career, I have been committed to delivering common-sense representation and real results. I believe elected officials should do more than identify challenges; they should work every day to address them. That commitment continues to guide my work as your City Councillor and Deputy Mayor.

Madhuri Azad is a socially active Scarborough-Agincourt resident, licensed Ontario lawyer, and an active community volunteer. She brings a professional experience of over 16 years in the legal field with a blend of technical and innovative skills gained through her background in Computer Science Engineering and an advanced degree in Master of Laws (LL.M.).

Through her community leadership, she contributes to local parent council governance, promotes parent/caregiver engagement to support student achievement, and focuses on advocating for students’ safety. Her work in these roles centers on bridging gaps to ensure parent voices directly shape educational resource allocation for students.

As an engaged resident, Madhuri Azad connects with the community through surveys and open discussions to understand local concerns, while also exploring a framework to establish a local Resident Welfare Association. Her combined experience, as a legal professional and community involved individual, focuses on regulatory frameworks, policy review, analysis, and advancing access to justice by demystifying the complex legal system for diverse community blocks.
She understands the system and knows how to fight for our kids and community. Together, let's elect a stronger voice this time.
Please Elect Madhuri Azad for city council in Ward 22 (Scarborough-Agincourt) for a strong voice advocating for families at Toronto City Hall.

answers.bio:
Darrell Brown has over three decades of consulting and legal experience, serving major multinational corporations, charities, not-for-profits, national and international unions, governments and their regulatory authorities, and institutions such as USAID and the Asian Development Bank. He has consulted in fifteen countries with oversight responsibilities for projects on five continents, and was awarded a medal and commendation from the Ukrainian government for his work on social sector reforms there.

Darrell has advised on a wide range of topics, including government relations, judicial reform, pensions, provident funds, insurance, mutual funds, commercial law, bankruptcy procedure, securities law, non-bank financial services, institutional governance, and tax policy. His executive, managerial, and project management experience spans strategy development, financial assessment, operational planning, human resources, public relations, and technical implementation and performance measurement.

Beyond his international and domestic consulting, Darrell has worked in the arts sector and owned an art gallery in Toronto. Some of his most rewarding work has come from helping people in need, directly and through charities he has advised, work that has saved lives and reunited families. Darrell is the proud father of five children — three boys and two girls — whose heritage reflects a cultural mosaic of Guyanese, Ukrainian, and Canadian ancestry. Among his most recent successes, he raised $15 million to help the CNE survive COVID and avoid insolvency; it now holds the largest surplus in its history.
answers.ward_commitment_target: Secured funding and a firm timeline for all-day frequent GO service on the Stouffville and Lakeshore East lines serving Ward 25 — the concrete transit win Scarborough residents can verify, not a vague promise.

explanations.arts_culture_support: There is a demonstrable cost/benefit produced from cultural activities. A dollar in produces multiple dollars out if structured correctly. Arts and culture keep a city vibrant.
explanations.av_conditions: Again, these are not mutually exclusive categories. Data disclosure and service obligations are essential. That said, we have to look at labour impact when speaking about anything autonomous.
explanations.budget_gap_first: Before asking residents for more or cutting services, prove the administrative and procurement discipline I've called for elsewhere is actually being applied. Professional project management and competitive contracting should close gaps before taxes or services are touched.
explanations.business_attraction: Same principle as the last answer: employers follow the same fundamentals residents need — affordable housing so workers can live near jobs, reliable transportation, safety, and a functioning public realm. Chasing individual companies with bespoke deals is a weaker, less durable strategy.
explanations.business_climate: Businesses locate where workers can get there, feel safe, and find space to grow, not where taxes are marginally lower. Scarborough's employment lands are already at risk from housing pressure; the real economic-development lever is transit, safety and infrastructure investment.
explanations.capital_project_delays: I've managed complex projects across five continents and helped turn around the CNE's finances. Toronto's overruns are a delivery-discipline problem. Rigorous project management, procurement and contracting stop cost blowouts before political scope changes make them worse.
explanations.capital_transparency: There is a serious transparency issue in Toronto and Ontario for that matter. We are years behind other jurisdictions on FOI and blanket publishing of contracts. Transparency breeds accountability.
explanations.construction_capacity: Boom-bust public capital spending is exactly the instability I've flagged elsewhere. It discourages contractors and workers from investing in local capacity. A stable, multi-year pipeline of public housing and infrastructure projects is what lets that capacity actually get built.
explanations.cycling_network: Finishing what's approved honours commitments already made and keeps momentum on safer , consistent with prioritizing transit, walking and cycling on constrained corridors. But further citywide reallocations should be evaluated case-by-case, not accelerated uniformly.
explanations.encampment_removal: Only if the offer is permanent housing with supports. Housing-first: once genuinely suitable, permanent housing is offered, remaining in an encampment isn't housing, it's warehousing. Offers must be real and permanent, not just shelter beds - pair any move with continued supports.
explanations.housing_as_of_right: Blanket as-of-right ignores real differences in transit access across wards. I support targeted, well-sited housing — including supportive and 'missing middle' housing — under adopted Secondary Plans, not one-size-fits-all rules overriding local context.
explanations.housing_city_role: Direct public ownership guarantees permanence for supportive housing: critical to solving homelessness. But scale requires all three levers: partnering with non-profits, financing private supply, and building directly wherever the market and non-profit sector alone can't deliver.
explanations.housing_cost_reduction: Blanket as-of-right zoning and stripped standards override local planning control and neighbourhood context. The lever that actually lowers cost without those trade-offs is fiscal: reduce development charges and parkland levies, especially for affordable and supportive housing.
explanations.housing_density_location: Density should follow transit capacity, not blanket citywide rules. Corridors and rapid-transit nodes can absorb growth appropriately; low-rise interior neighbourhoods with poor transit access, like much of Scarborough, cannot without straining roads, parking and services.
explanations.housing_intervention: Zoning permissions and faster approvals won't produce deeply affordable or supportive housing on their own. The market doesn't build it. Solving homelessness means the city directly building and financing it. Public delivery is the lever within Council's control that gets people housed.
explanations.infrastructure_backlog: SOGR and expansion competing for the same pool is exactly the structural funding gap I've flagged before. The fix is a dedicated, protected maintenance revenue stream, not an annual scramble that leaves repair losing to ribbon-cuttings.
explanations.infrastructure_revenue: I have a comprehensive proposal on alternative revenue sources. Property tax revenue cannot service the needs of Torontonians. See my presentation at electdarrellbrown.ca
explanations.performance_metric: This is a loaded question. There should be multiple measures - housing, fiscal sustainability and specific measurable results at the ward level. A mayor has to lead on multiple fronts.
explanations.police_budget: Public safety funding should follow function, not headcount. Calls rooted in mental health, addiction and youth crisis are better and more safely handled by trained civilian responders — freeing police to focus on core policing, and delivering the crisis investment I outlined above.
explanations.property_tax_growth: Property tax should track cost and growth, not become the default lever for new priorities. The investments I've proposed: supportive housing, crisis services, transit should be funded through provincial/federal cost-sharing and dedicated tools like congestion pricing, not property tax hikes.
explanations.protest_access: The same principle I've applied to surveillance and data governance applies here: neither blanket restriction nor unlimited disruption, but clear, published rules on locations, access routes and duration that protect the right to protest while keeping essential services running.
explanations.provincial_approach: The province's TTC operating contribution sits near 9%, much of it one-off. That structural imbalance won't fix itself. Toronto needs to publicly press for a standing funding formula and real fiscal tools, not quietly align with provincial priorities hoping for scraps.
explanations.public_realm_priority: This is the same principle as my infrastructure-backlog answer: protect the basics first. Clean, well-maintained roads, sidewalks, parks and washrooms are what residents actually rely on daily before the city commits to fewer, flashier signature projects.
explanations.revenue_source: Congestion charges and road-use fees put the cost on those who create it, fund transit and street investment directly, and avoid the trade-offs of higher property tax or development charges. However, municipal income tax is a progressive tax and is more affordable.
explanations.road_pricing: Congestion pricing has worked to reduce traffic by up to 30% (London). New York and Singapore are examples of success. How it is structured is key.
explanations.safety_investment: Enforcement manages crises after they happen; crisis and prevention services stop them from happening. Mental-health response, addiction treatment and youth intervention are the same 'treatment first' logic behind my homelessness plan — investing upstream reduces the burden downstream.
explanations.service_delivery_model: Competitive procurement and outside delivery, tested against real service standards, is the same discipline behind the professional project management I called for above. Where the city does use arm's-length agencies, they need the same conflict-of-interest safeguards I've proposed elsewhere.
explanations.street_space_priority: Transit, walking and cycling move the most people per metre of street. It is the logic behind the BRT corridors (dedicated lanes, signal priority) I've proposed. Neighbourhood parking needs are addressed separately, through building-level requirements, not general curb allocation.
explanations.strong_mayor_powers: Strong mayor powers shouldn't override Council's collective judgment on housing or budget. That's the concentrated authority my transparency work warns against. The legitimate use is internal management: staffing decisions and departmental restructuring.
explanations.surveillance_tech: Surveillance tools need the same accountability infrastructure I've proposed for FOI and conflict-of-interest reform: clear citywide rules on access, retention, auditing and data-sharing, adopted by Council directly rather than left to weak existing privacy law.
explanations.technology_investment: Public data and performance-measurement systems are the technology backbone of the FOI/COI reforms I've proposed — proactive disclosure, municipal scorecards and departmental accountability all depend on the city actually being able to measure and publish what departments do.
explanations.transit_funding_priority: We can't wait for the next multi-decade build. Treating existing GO corridors as real rapid transit now, with frequent all-day service and fare integration, delivers benefits years before subway extensions open — and it's the lever the city can actually pull today.
explanations.ward_commitment_target: The problem with surveys is that questions can be framed to artificially narrow choices. A fundamental point to many of my proposed solutions is integration of currently isolated programs, creating efficiencies without necessarily increasing costs.
explanations.ward_objective: Scarborough absorbs a growing share of the city's development without matching investment in transit, roads, parks and local infrastructure. Ward 25's next term should close that gap before adding further growth pressure the current infrastructure can't support.

Shelley Carroll has spent her career helping build stronger communities.

Before entering public life, Shelley owned and operated a small business while raising her family in North York. She was an active volunteer in her daughters' school community, helping lead breakfast programs and organizing against funding cuts to public education. Those experiences shaped her belief that strong communities are built by people who step up, listen, and work together.

That commitment to public service led Shelley from School Trustee to Toronto City Council, where she has proudly represented Don Valley North for more than 20 years.

Today, Shelley is one of Toronto’s most experienced civic leaders. She currently serves as Budget Chief, the Mayor’s Economic Development and Culture Champion, and Chair of the Toronto Police Service Board, helping lead the city through some of its biggest financial, economic, and public safety challenges.

Whether she’s advocating for safer neighbourhoods, improving parks and community spaces, supporting local businesses, or helping residents navigate City Hall, Shelley is known for thoughtful leadership, strong relationships, and delivering results for the community she calls home.

explanations.housing_city_role: Toronto’s primary job is to enable housing by approving enough homes and removing unnecessary barriers to construction. But a city of our size should also use every tool available from regulation to public land and partnerships to make sure we are building the homes our residents need.
explanations.housing_intervention: We need to build more affordable and supportive housing people can actually afford. That means working with other levels of government and non-profit partners to build homes, create jobs and invest in the infrastructure our communities need.
explanations.infrastructure_revenue: Toronto cannot afford to defer critical infrastructure repairs, but we should prioritize finding efficiencies and making full use of existing revenue tools while pressing the provincial and federal governments for their fair share of infrastructure funding.
explanations.provincial_approach: We've demonstrated that Toronto is a willing partner, but as the city we are left to operate the asset so we need new funding arrangements.
explanations.road_pricing: Road pricing is only an option if it is fair, equitable and regional in scope. Any such system would need to be developed in partnership with other levels of government, and should be publicly owned and publicly operated so all the revenue will make its way to transportation improvements.
explanations.safety_investment: We need to invest more in crisis prevention, mental-health response, addiction treatment and youth intervention while maintaining our current levels of investment in the enforcement and public-space management that keep our communities safe.
explanations.service_delivery_model: We need to continuously strengthen Toronto’s project management capacity so major projects are delivered on time, on budget and with clear accountability to taxpayers.
explanations.street_space_priority: Our priority should be moving people and essential goods efficiently. If we get passenger capacity and essential access right, general traffic and parking will follow.
explanations.strong_mayor_powers: We've learned over time that every mayor has had to work with Council to build support for major priorities. The tools to lead on administration, budgeting and housing are already available under the City of Toronto Act, but building consensus sets these up for success.
explanations.transit_funding_priority: We need to make the service we have right now much more reliable than it is today. That will improve our ridership and help us generate expansion. We also need to get the Sheppard Subway expansion built!

answers.bio: Braeden Chow is a Toronto nonprofit founder, musician and community organizer running for Mayor to bring urgency, accountability and imagination back to City Hall. He believes Toronto should be safer, more affordable and more ambitious about its future.
answers.ward_commitment_target: Complete the first phase of heated-road infrastructure across Ward 9 by December 2026, subject to technical approval and community support, before expanding the program to any other ward.

explanations.arts_culture_support: Protection from displacement. Toronto doesn’t need more venues for the sake of having more venues. It should focus on preserving established cultural spaces that already contribute to their communities and the city’s identity.
explanations.av_conditions: Toronto should explore operating or owning its own autonomous taxi service, so the City can control pricing, accessibility, coverage, safety standards and potentially keep the revenue public.
explanations.budget_gap_first: Reduce or redesign lower-priority services first. A structural deficit usually signals a management problem. Essential services should be protected, contracts should deliver strong value, and residents shouldn’t be asked to pay more before the City fixes its own spending.
explanations.business_attraction: Strong citywide fundamentals matter, but when you’re competing for a major employer, investment or event, Toronto should be willing to put together a tailored package and actively win the opportunity instead of assuming it will come here on its own.
explanations.business_climate: Lower costs. Strong fundamentals matter, but businesses also need room to operate. Toronto should reduce unnecessary taxes, fees and licensing costs while maintaining the infrastructure, safety and services that make the city competitive.
explanations.capital_project_delays: The right team with strong project management, procurement and contracting should be able to deliver ambitious projects without constantly shrinking the pipeline. Councillors also shouldn’t be casually changing scope midstream, but execution is the bigger issue.
explanations.capital_transparency: I support accountability, but not publishing endless reports that most people will never use. Major overruns and failures should be disclosed clearly, but City Hall should focus on delivering projects, not creating more bureaucracy around them.
explanations.construction_capacity: If Toronto doesn’t have enough skilled people to actually do the work, everything else slows down. Expanding apprenticeships, training and recognition of international credentials increases the number of qualified workers without lowering standards.
explanations.cycling_network: Toronto should finish what it has already approved, assess how those projects actually perform, and avoid constantly reallocating more road space until we know the existing network is working well for cyclists, drivers, businesses and local communities.
explanations.encampment_removal: Yes. If the City has offered a genuinely available indoor space that meets the person’s accessibility, safety and household needs, I believe they should be required to leave the encampment. Parks are public spaces and need to remain safe and accessible for everyone.
explanations.housing_as_of_right: support building substantially more housing across Toronto, but I wouldn’t say every ward needs the exact same level or type of development. Housing policy should reflect local infrastructure, transit, neighbourhood context and actual capacity. We need more homes, but we also need smart planning.
explanations.housing_city_role: Toronto should take more responsibility itself: build, acquire, and own more affordable/supportive housing, rather than mainly relying on private developers or outside partners to solve the problem.
explanations.housing_cost_reduction: weakening the standards that determine who can build, where they can build, and whether the project is actually appropriate. Faster shouldn’t mean automatic approval for anyone with a proposal.
explanations.housing_density_location: I’d concentrate the greatest density increases downtown and in existing growth centres. Toronto is large enough that every neighbourhood doesn’t need the same built form.
explanations.housing_intervention: We need more affordable and supportive housing, but I don’t support simply opening the door for anyone to build anything anywhere.
explanations.infrastructure_backlog: Before raising another levy or selling off public assets, the City should make sure it can properly maintain what it already owns. New projects are great, but not if existing roads, facilities and infrastructure are falling apart because money is spread too thin.
explanations.infrastructure_revenue: I don’t think the first answer should be raising more revenue. Toronto already collects a significant amount of money, and before asking residents to pay more, the City should prove it is spending what it has efficiently, prioritizing essential repairs properly, and reducing waste.
explanations.performance_metric: Public realm. Safer, cleaner, better-maintained streets and public spaces depend on strong services and responsible finances. If the City is managed properly, residents should see and feel the results in their everyday lives.
explanations.police_budget: increase above inflation, but not simply to hire more officers. I want a stronger, better-trained, better-equipped force with serious mental-health, recovery and family support off duty. Police deal with extraordinary situations; we should invest in keeping them capable and healthy.
explanations.property_tax_growth: I’d lean grow more slowly than inflation. Property taxes shouldn’t automatically rise just because costs do. The City should first find efficiencies and spend better. If a genuine need remains, increases around inflation can be justified.
explanations.protest_access: Maintaining access. Peaceful protest should be protected, but it should not prevent people from reaching hospitals, using transit, getting to work or accessing essential services. Public expression matters, but so does keeping the city functioning safely.
explanations.provincial_approach: Partnership. Toronto should work constructively with whatever provincial government is elected when doing so gets the city funding, approvals or better outcomes. I’m not interested in fighting Queen’s Park for the sake of it, but I also wouldn’t accept a bad deal just to say we cooperated.
explanations.public_realm_priority: Programming and activity. I want major events and cultural programming concentrated where they make sense, generating revenue and supporting local business, while still letting residential neighbourhoods stay calm, clean and enjoyable to live in.
explanations.revenue_source: A balanced mix makes more sense, while also growing non-tax revenue through events, tourism, sponsorships, venue use and other economic activity so the City isn’t constantly reaching deeper into residents’ pockets.
explanations.road_pricing: I don’t support charging residents for congestion when so much of it is caused by construction, lane closures, poor coordination and inadequate infrastructure. The City should fix the congestion problems within its control before making drivers pay for them.
explanations.safety_investment: I’d choose public-space management, but safety can’t be reduced to visibility alone. Police also need the resources, staffing and tools to actually prevent and respond to crime. The goal should be safer residents and officers, not simply more uniforms on the street.
explanations.service_delivery_model: I’d use competitive outside providers where they can deliver better value, but only with strict performance standards and real accountability. If a contractor is doing a bad job, the City should be able to replace them quickly rather than being stuck with poor service.
explanations.street_space_priority: I’d prioritize goods and essential access. Deliveries, trades, emergency services and accessibility are foundational to how the city functions. When space is limited, the people and services that keep Toronto operating should come first.
explanations.strong_mayor_powers: Budget. If voters elect a mayor with a clear mandate, that mayor should be able to set spending and tax priorities and be held accountable for the results. Administrative powers should be used carefully, not as a tool for constantly reshuffling City staff.
explanations.surveillance_tech: I’d permit broad use under existing privacy law. If technology can help police find stolen vehicles, identify serious offenders and solve crimes faster, we should use it. For law-abiding residents, effective public-safety tools should make the city safer, not harder to live in.
explanations.technology_investment: Toronto should use technology to make City Hall faster, smarter and more efficient behind the scenes. Better procurement, staffing and financial systems can improve services without weakening standards or accountability.
explanations.transit_funding_priority: I’d prioritize service. Riders need more frequent, reliable and safer transit they can actually count on every day. Maintenance matters, but the greatest share should go toward improving the day-to-day experience for people using the system.
explanations.ward_commitment_target: This survey was too generalized for many of the questions. Toronto is a large, diverse city, and different areas require different solutions based on their infrastructure, population, services, finances and actual needs.
explanations.ward_objective: Keeping Ward 9 safe is the priority. It is already a strong community, and I want to protect that while making our parks, streets and public spaces substantially better. explanations.av_conditions: If autonomous taxis operate in Toronto, accessibility and equitable service must come first. Services should accommodate people with disabilities, meet clear safety and service standards, and provide fair geographic coverage so communities are not left behind.
explanations.budget_gap_first: Before asking residents to pay more or reducing essential services, Toronto should examine administrative spending, contracts and internal efficiencies. Any savings should protect frontline workers and the services residents rely on while ensuring public dollars are used responsibly.
explanations.business_attraction: Toronto attracts investment when it is a city where people want and can afford to live and work. We should strengthen housing affordability, transportation, public safety, infrastructure and quality of life, creating conditions where businesses, workers and communities can succeed.
explanations.business_climate: A strong business climate depends on strong communities. Toronto should improve housing, reliable transportation, public safety and infrastructure while supporting local businesses. explanations.capital_project_delays: Toronto needs stronger project management, procurement and oversight to keep major projects on time and on budget. Residents deserve clear accountability for delays and cost overruns and confidence that public dollars are being managed responsibly.
explanations.capital_transparency: Yes. Residents deserve transparency about how public dollars are being spent. Major capital projects should have clear, accessible information on budgets, timelines, delays and performance so residents can track progress and hold the City accountable for results.
explanations.construction_capacity: Toronto should invest in its people by expanding apprenticeships, skilled-trades training and pathways for internationally trained workers. explanations.cycling_network: Toronto should complete its approved cycling projects while ensuring future changes are guided by safety, local needs and evidence. explanations.encampment_removal: Yes. Everyone deserves to be treated with dignity and compassion. explanations.housing_as_of_right: Yes. Toronto needs more housing in every ward, but growth must be responsible and supported by adequate infrastructure. explanations.housing_city_role: Toronto should use City land, funding and incentives to expand affordable and supportive housing through strong partnerships with non-profit and community housing providers, while also maintaining a direct role where City ownership can protect long-term affordability.
explanations.housing_cost_reduction: Toronto should reduce unnecessary delays and make routine approvals more efficient while maintaining strong standards for safety and responsible development. explanations.housing_density_location: The greatest density should be located near rapid transit and major corridors where residents can more easily access jobs and services. explanations.housing_intervention: Public delivery: Toronto needs more housing that people can actually afford. explanations.infrastructure_backlog: Toronto needs a reliable, dedicated approach to maintaining roads, sidewalks, facilities and other critical infrastructure. explanations.police_budget: Toronto needs effective policing alongside stronger prevention and community supports. Police should focus on serious crime and public safety, while we strengthen community-based mental health and crisis response, youth intervention and prevention services.

explanations.provincial_approach: Toronto should work constructively with the Province to secure funding and advance priorities that benefit residents, while continuing to advocate firmly for Toronto’s needs. explanations.public_realm_priority: Residents deserve clean, safe and well-maintained neighbourhoods. explanations.road_pricing: No. Transportation improvements need sustainable funding, but additional charges should not increase costs for residents already struggling with affordability. explanations.safety_investment: Public safety requires prevention as well as enforcement. explanations.street_space_priority: Transit, walking and cycling should generally be prioritized so more people can move safely and efficiently. explanations.strong_mayor_powers: If strong mayor powers are used, they should be exercised cautiously and transparently. Housing is an urgent priority, but decisions must still consider affordability, infrastructure, community needs and the voices of residents affected by development.
explanations.surveillance_tech: Technology can support public safety, but its use must be balanced with residents’ privacy and individual rights. Toronto should establish clear rules on data collection, access, retention and sharing, with strong oversight and accountability to prevent misuse.
explanations.technology_investment: Technology should make City services easier and faster for residents to access. explanations.transit_funding_priority: Reliable transit is essential for residents getting to work, school, appointments and essential services. explanations.ward_objective: Ward 7 needs more housing and investment, but growth must benefit existing residents. I support affordable and family-sized housing, responsible development and local jobs, while ensuring our streets, roads, parks and public spaces are safe, clean and well maintained.

answers.bio:
Born in Ontario, I have called Toronto home since I was five. School, work and life have taken me across the city, shaping my belief that Toronto is much more than its downtown core. I believe understanding this city means getting outside your own neighbourhood, routine and bubble, and experiencing Toronto through the lives of friends, family and the people who call its many neighbourhoods home. I’m the son of a Portuguese father and Italian mother, and grew up surrounded by the cultures, neighbourhoods and small businesses that are such a big part of Toronto’s identity. My friends and I have joked for years about me becoming mayor, partly because of my personality, but mostly because I never seem to stop talking about cities. Whether I’m at home or travelling, I’m always pointing something out: Why can’t we do this in Toronto? Who thought that was a good idea?

This curiosity about cities eventually led me to graduate studies in environmental studies and urban planning. It gave me a stronger foundation for looking at housing, transportation, public space, the environment and city government as connected pieces rather than separate problems. I think that perspective can help me bring meaningful, practical and sometimes unconventional ideas to City Hall. I may not be the most familiar name running for mayor. That’s kind of the point. I’m running because sometimes the person willing to ask why we keep doing things the same way is exactly the person worth giving a chance.

explanations.arts_culture_support: We’ve lost too many great Toronto spaces only to see an empty storefront or another chain replace them. There’s no one-tool solution: we need easier rules for nightlife and culture, plus ideas like 24-hour subway service on weekends so people can stay out and actually get home easily.
explanations.av_conditions: If they’re here, we need to know how they’re affecting congestion, safety and our streets. Toronto has bigger transportation issues to tackle first. Autonomous taxis don’t need to be a priority right now.
explanations.budget_gap_first: Look for administrative inefficiencies and poor value contracts first, without weakening frontline services or the city’s in house capacity.
explanations.business_attraction: Make Toronto a city where people actually want to live, work and invest. We should also target sectors where Toronto has an advantage and work with other governments on major opportunities.
explanations.business_climate: Better streets, transportation and infrastructure help businesses thrive, but so do faster approvals, less unnecessary red tape and actually listening to businesses about what they need.
explanations.capital_project_delays: Toronto is pretty good at announcing things. We need to get much better at actually delivering them.
explanations.capital_transparency: Torontonians shouldn't need a detective's license to figure out why a project is late or over budget.
explanations.construction_capacity: Toronto should try modular construction, and other ways to build faster and more efficiently. But efficiency shouldn’t mean sacrificing good design or building the same thing everywhere. Workforce training and recognizing international credentials matter too, with senior governments leading
explanations.cycling_network: Finish and strengthen what we have, especially while the Province continues to interfere with bike lanes. I don’t want Toronto spending money on infrastructure that could just be ripped up.
explanations.encampment_removal: I would say it’s conditional on the premise being true. We cannot demand people leave if suitable alternatives aren’t available. If we provide an appropriate indoor option that meets someone’s needs, I don’t believe an encampment in a shared public space should become permanent.
explanations.housing_as_of_right: Every neighbourhood needs to be accommodating more housing, particularly missing middle and gentle density approaches. But as a planner, I’m weary of identical built forms everywhere. Good cities need variety, character and housing choice.
explanations.housing_city_role: Toronto should use its land, funding and municipal tools to dramatically expand affordable and supportive housing through strong partnerships with non-profits, co-ops and other housing providers, while retaining direct public delivery where it makes sense.
explanations.housing_cost_reduction: If a project follows the rules, it shouldn’t take forever to get a permit. I’m also open to reducing unnecessary requirements like parking minimums, but Toronto isn’t in a position to simply give up revenue needed to accommodate growth.
explanations.housing_density_location: Concentrating more growth in a few centres puts pressure on local infrastructure, services and public spaces. The next frontier is gentle density. More multiplexes, townhomes and small apartments in residential neighbourhoods, so more of the city participates in solving our housing shortage.
explanations.housing_intervention: We need all three, but permission has the broadest citywide impact. We can’t address housing scarcity while large parts of Toronto remain difficult to build apartments in. More than a handful of wards are actually losing population while the city as a whole continues to grow.
explanations.infrastructure_backlog: Before asking residents for more, we should prioritize maintaining what we already have. That doesn’t mean stop building new things. We should be smarter about what’s built and explore new ways to fund new projects. Money towards other public realm improvements.
explanations.infrastructure_revenue: Deferring maintenance just means a bigger bill later. Toronto should fight for its fair share from other governments, but also take responsibility for maintaining its infrastructure.
explanations.performance_metric: The test is pretty simple: does Toronto feel better than it did four years ago? Better streets and public spaces, more life, more fun, fewer “why on earth did we do that?” moments. A city that feels functional, a city that feels worth it.
explanations.police_budget: Keep police properly funded and keeping pace with inflation, while putting new investments into civilian crisis services.
explanations.property_tax_growth: But we need to stop treating property taxes as the answer to everything. Toronto needs a real conversation about other ways to raise revenue that don’t keep asking the average resident to pay more.
explanations.protest_access: Protect the right to protest, but have clear rules so essential access and services aren’t disrupted.
explanations.provincial_approach: Work with Queen’s Park when it benefits Toronto, absolutely, but don’t be afraid to stand up for our city. For too long, Toronto has quietly pushed back, conceded or compromised one priority for another. We need greater authority, new revenue tools and be prepared to go it alone when needed.
explanations.public_realm_priority: Let’s create better streets, parks and public spaces, and then bring them to life with markets, patios, events and cultural programming. The two should go hand in hand.
explanations.revenue_source: This doesn’t mean rushing into congestion pricing. I’d rather explore targeted options, like a commercial parking levy, before falling back on broad tax increases on residents. Let’s also be willing to look at new revenue models and have that conversation.
explanations.road_pricing: I understand the planning case for congestion pricing, and Toronto can explore it down the line. But right now, I’d rather focus on improvements people use every day. Better TTC service, faster streetcars and making transit an even better alternative to driving. Give people better choices first.
explanations.safety_investment: Let police focus on policing. Expanding mental-health, addiction and crisis services means the right professionals can respond to the right situations, while freeing up police resources for public safety.
explanations.service_delivery_model: Contracting something out doesn’t magically make it cheaper or better. Toronto’s garbage collection experience is a good example… Keep strong in-house capacity and outsource when it actually makes sense.
explanations.street_space_priority: Our streets should prioritize moving people efficiently, while protecting essential and accessibility needs. We should also be more creative with our streets. This includes pedestrianization in places like Queen, Church and Kensington Market, where sidewalks often leave little room for people.
explanations.strong_mayor_powers: I am cautious about strong-mayor powers and would rather build support at Council. But housing is where I see the strongest case for using them. I’d also use administrative authority where needed to bring more ambitious, creative thinking into City Hall.
explanations.surveillance_tech: There are legitimate public-safety uses for this technology, but that doesn’t justify creating a permanent database of everyone’s movements. Clear limits on access, retention and data sharing are essential.
explanations.technology_investment: Make it easier and faster for people to actually deal with the City.. Permits, licences, payments and service requests shouldn’t be a headache.
explanations.transit_funding_priority: A reliable transit system starts with taking care of what we already have. Service improvements are also a priority, but they depend on a system that works.
explanations.ward_objective: Toronto is growing, but the basics need to keep up. Better transit, streets, parks and infrastructure are what make that growth actually work for people.

Before deciding to run for mayor, Laura was a partner at a well-known Bay Street law firm where she worked as a municipal and land use planning lawyer for over a decade. Laura has been involved in development applications across Toronto and has firsthand experience working with City departments to move projects from concept to construction. Councils, residents, and private-sector clients across Ontario trusted Laura for legal advice on pressing municipal issues.

Laura believes in civility, accountability, and transparency in government and has acted as an Integrity Commissioner and Closed Meeting Investigator for municipalities throughout the province.

Before law, Laura worked inside the Ontario government as a Senior Policy Advisor in the Housing Policy branch of the Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing, and previously as a Policy Analyst in the Climate Change Secretariat at Cabinet Office.

Currently, Laura is on the Board of the Friends of Allan Gardens, a registered charity dedicated to revitalizing the historic park and conservatories. Laura was previously a volunteer with Cycle Toronto, winning Volunteer of the Year in 2017 for her advocacy on the Bloor Street bike lane. Laura also volunteered for many years with the Canadian Red Cross' Street Relief program, providing weekly hot meals at Sherbourne and Wellesley.

explanations.arts_culture_support: Arts and culture are vital to Toronto but have had to adapt to an ever-changing city. To ensure the continued survival of arts and culture, the City must be a partner, not a barrier. It must provide space, enable permitting and alter regulations so our cultural sector can thrive here.
explanations.av_conditions: The City should not stand in the way of autonomous taxis if residents are in favour of this service.
explanations.budget_gap_first: Changes with the least impact on Torontonian's day-to-day experiences must be prioritized.
explanations.business_climate: City departments often do not talk to each other or have overlapping functions. I have seen firsthand how this impacts small businesses, costing time and money.
explanations.capital_project_delays: Contractors must be held to project timelines and specifications.
explanations.capital_transparency: Accountability requires transparency. The public should not have to file freedom of information requests to understand how their money is being spent by the City.
explanations.construction_capacity: A shortage of skilled labor creates an immediate bottleneck to increasing construction capacity. The City needs to work with trade schools and other partners to address this issue.
explanations.cycling_network: To maximize the City's investment in existing cycling infrastructure, new bike lanes should be installed where there is demonstrated demand and where they provide missing links to the larger cycling network.
explanations.encampment_removal: Public parks are finite public resources which were not designed for long-term habitation. I would support requiring a person to leave an encampment where the new accommodation offers a viable path towards stable housing but not where it would only result in eventual relocation to a different park.
explanations.housing_as_of_right: Toronto already permits up to 4 residential units as-of-right in Neighbourhoods while six-plexes are legal in select wards. I support these intensification policies but believe substantially more housing as-of-right ("upzoning") needs to be directed to Avenues and major transit station areas.
explanations.housing_city_role: Non-profit and private providers have a better track record of delivering projects than the City. The City should rely on its ability to supply land, funding and incentives and leave the work of building, acquiring and owning the housing to its expert partners.
explanations.housing_cost_reduction: Faster approvals only address part of the problem. Once a project is approved, it requires the City and the owner to enter into various agreements. The process for these agreements is incredibly and leads to construction delays. This internal process can be improved.
explanations.housing_density_location: Each Toronto neighbourhood has its own character.  City Planning must recognize the uniqueness of each area when deciding where to permit increases in density. Designating major streets and transit for intensification maximizes public infrastructure and avoids disrupting stable neighbourhoods.
explanations.housing_intervention: Reducing DCs and updating zoning permissions are important for new housing but will not solve the affordable housing crisis. Next term, the City should focus on building and financing the deeply affordable and supportive housing that market solutions cannot provide.
explanations.infrastructure_backlog: The money Toronto will save by no longer having financial and operational responsibility for the DVP and Gardiner should be reserved for addressing Toronto's infrastructure backlog.
explanations.infrastructure_revenue: Today's Torontonians should not have to shoulder the burden of years of neglected maintenance through increased property taxes. Given the City's economic and cultural importance to the rest of the province and country, Toronto deserves its fair share of infrastructure funding from other governments.
explanations.police_budget: TPS should focus its resources on reducing the number of guns on the street and addressing violent crime.
explanations.property_tax_growth: Taxes were raised last term and should remain stable over the next council term.
explanations.protest_access: I support the right to peaceful assembly guaranteed by the Charter, subject to reasonable limits which would likely include keeping major roads, transit, hospitals and essential institutions operating.
explanations.provincial_approach: Toronto has little legal authority to prevent provincial interference.  It is in the long-term interest of Torontonians to partner with the province for funding and approvals. If, however a provincial initiative threatens our priorities, advocacy is essential to protecting Torontonians.
explanations.public_realm_priority: Without programming, the City's investments our parks and other spaces cannot be fully realized. Programming pays dividends in terms of local economic benefit and social connection and ensures the City maximizes its investment in public spaces.
explanations.revenue_source: Road charges won't happen politically. Land transfer taxes and development charges ultimately harm the purchaser. Property taxes are the City's most reliable source of revenue.
explanations.road_pricing: The road pricing question is not worth spending much time on because this provincial government will never allow Toronto to implement road tolls. In theory, I would be very supportive of Toronto implementing a congestion charge in the downtown core for non-residents or tiered pricing.
explanations.safety_investment: Mental health and addiction issues are in plain view in Toronto's public spaces, making us feel uncomfortable and sometimes unsafe. More trained crisis intervention workers are needed, especially on the TTC. Youth must be given job and leadership opportunities so they can find purpose and identity.
explanations.service_delivery_model: Where it can be demonstrated that a private company could deliver better value to Torontonians, external delivery should be used. However, Toronto's experience with waste collection demonstrates that external delivery is not guaranteed to lead to savings or better service.
explanations.street_space_priority: Streets are for people and should be able to move as many people as safely as possible.
explanations.strong_mayor_powers: Strong Mayor powers should be used where Council stands in the way of crucial housing getting built.  Overall budget decisions impacting the City as a whole as well as decisions on senior staff and departments should be made and owned by all of Council.
explanations.surveillance_tech: With strict protections, automated licence-plate readers and similar surveillance technology have the potential to benefit Torontonians.
explanations.technology_investment: Technology improvements should be directed towards identifying cost savings in the delivery of services and maintenance/repair of City assets.
explanations.transit_funding_priority: Many people choose to drive because they are not confident the TTC will get them to where they are going on time. Better reliability is key to reducing congestion.
explanations.ward_objective: We need to focus on making Toronto better, easier and more beautiful for Torontonians.

Andi Hoàng-Lefranc was born and raised in Toronto to a working-class family and now calls Spadina-Fort York home. As a former public servant and lawyer, Andi has always prioritised service through action and as your neighbour they know first-hand the pressures you are facing.

The pressures Ward 10 faces are no small challenge but big problems deserve brave actions and Andi is prepared to use every tool at their disposal to make life in Spadina-Fort York affordable so that you can thrive.

In their spare time, you can find Andi running, brushing up on legal theory, making saves as a goalkeeper, or cheering on AFC Toronto. explanations.capital_project_delays: Major infrastructure projects often face delays and cost overruns due to a lack of actual fiscal oversight and transparency as to how resources are used. Strengthening professional project management, procurement, and contracting is integral to ensuring projects are delivered on time and on budget.
explanations.capital_transparency: Torontonians deserve transparency on how their tax dollars are being utilised, especially when concerning major capital projects. Disclosing project-level budgets, schedules, and performance updates to the public is a good start towards strengthening the relationship between residents and Council.
explanations.encampment_removal: In addition to accessibility, safety and household needs, the City must also consider the unique social needs of our houseless residents. Strict requirements to leave an encampment, without consideration of homeless residents' social support needs will only result in further housing instability.
explanations.housing_as_of_right: As Toronto continues to grow and expand, residents have been forced into living arrangements and accommodations that do not reflect how the land is currently zoned as. Permitting more housing as-of-right in every ward will give the City a better understanding of its residents housing needs.
explanations.housing_city_role: Non-profit housing providers & community land trusts best understand the unique housing needs of the communities they serve. By partnering with them, the City can best ensure that any new affordable & supportive housing is actually able to meet the everyday needs of its residents.
explanations.housing_cost_reduction: The slow pace of the city's administrative process is routinely mentioned by tenants, architects, and developers as the primary issue in delivering affordable housing. Expanding as-of-right zoning & automating routine permits will address this issue directly while reducing administrative costs.
explanations.housing_density_location: Lack of housing is an issue that affects the entire city, not just one specific neighbourhood. As the City's transit network continues to expand and Toronto becomes  increasingly interconnected, increasing the City's overall housing supply will best take advantage of this interconnectivity.
explanations.housing_intervention: There are many non-profit housing providers & community land trusts who have not been able to access needed funds to support the housing requirements of their communities. City Council must better fund Toronto's Multi-Unit Residential Acquisition (MURA) program to better partner with such groups.
explanations.infrastructure_backlog: Public infrastructure repair and maintenance cannot be addressed as an ad-hoc issue. Having a dedicated revenue source to address the city's infrastructure repair backlog as soon as possible, will allow us to avoid more costly future infrastructure repairs that could have been avoided.
explanations.infrastructure_revenue: In our political & economic climate, Toronto must look into independent local revenue sources as productive collaboration between different levels of government cannot be guaranteed. Residents and other civic bodies are being asked to do more with less, the City of Toronto should do the same.
explanations.performance_metric: There is no one metric that can be used to accurately assess a City Councillor's performance. Rather, at the end of the term residents should ask themselves whether their quality of life has improved from four years ago as a result of their councillor's actions and initiatives.
explanations.police_budget: The TPS are currently tasked with multiple non-policing duties which make it difficult for the TPS to fulfil their mandate. By delegating these extraneous duties to other city bodies and services, it will better allow police to focus on their role as a civic partner in maintaining public safety.
explanations.property_tax_growth: In our uncertain economic climate, the City can best support its residents by offering stable and predictable governance. By indexing residential property-taxes to inflation and population growth, residents are better able to manage their financial futures as economic and political challenges arise.
explanations.provincial_approach: In our current political climate, productive collaboration between municipal and provincial governments is not guaranteed. In consideration of this political reality, Toronto must be better prepared to independently deliver municipal services, regardless of whether provincial support is provided.
explanations.revenue_source: The City must find a way to collaborate with individuals & private groups who rely heavily on Toronto's road network for their transportation needs. User and road charges can be part of this collaboration, only if the revenue is invested towards improving the city's road and traffic infrastructure.
explanations.road_pricing: Introducing road-pricing measures should only be one tool in the City's bid to reduce overall congestion. Applying the revenue generated from these measures towards transportation improvements, such as better roads and upgraded signal prioritisation, will improve how residents navigate our city.
explanations.safety_investment: To improve public safety, the City must address the root social causes that contribute to the rise of mental-health crises, addiction rates, & youth violence. Stronger enforcement in response to public safety that ignores these causes will only lead to short-term public safety improvements.
explanations.service_delivery_model: While private parties can provide good service value, it doesn't mean it's the most cost-effective way to deliver city services. The focus of a business is to provide services while generating profit whereas the role of a city is to deliver city services within a budget provided by its residents.
explanations.street_space_priority: In order for Toronto to function, residents must be able to navigate around the City easily and efficiently. By prioritising moving the most amount of people as safely as possible, this will relieve traffic congestion while allowing people to fulfil their social, professional, & commercial needs.
explanations.strong_mayor_powers: The use of strong mayor powers must be limited to the scope of their purpose which is to encourage collaboration on shared priorities between the municipal and provincial governments. As Toronto faces a housing crisis, the use of such powers to encourage housing development should be considered.
explanations.surveillance_tech: The broad use of surveillance technology upon the general public should be limited as much as possible. Residents' right to privacy is paramount in a society where malicious actors seek to take advantage of a person's private details for nefarious purposes, such as identify fraud and stalking.
explanations.transit_funding_priority: Clean and working public transit infrastructure is a critical requirement to improve transit service reliability. Without functional vehicles, accessible stations, or an intelligent signal prioritisation system, providing more reliable transit service is not possible.
explanations.ward_commitment_target: There is no one metric that can be used to accurately assess a City Councillor's performance. Rather, at the end of the term residents should ask themselves whether their quality of life has improved from four years ago as a result of their councillor's actions and initiatives.
explanations.ward_objective: Spadina-Fort York is more than just a neighbourhood where people live. The ward is also host to large scale sporting & entertainment events and major conferences. This requires improved people and public space management so that residents and visitors are able to feel safe and welcomed in the ward.
