explanations.arts_culture_support: Toronto should support arts, culture and nightlife by simplifying permits, reducing unnecessary barriers and creating flexible rules that help artists, venues and cultural businesses thrive while respecting neighbourhoods and public safety.
explanations.av_conditions: Autonomous taxis should serve all Torontonians fairly. The City should prioritize accessibility, city-wide coverage and reliable service standards, while ensuring safety and preventing technology from creating new gaps in mobility.
explanations.budget_gap_first: Toronto should address budget gaps first by improving efficiency, reducing unnecessary administrative and contract costs, and eliminating waste. Essential frontline services should be protected, and higher taxes should be a last resort.
explanations.business_attraction: Toronto should attract investment by building strong fundamentals: affordable housing, efficient transportation, safe communities and a high quality of life. A well-planned, livable city naturally attracts employers, talent and major events.
explanations.business_climate: Toronto should become a faster and more predictable place to invest. Streamlining permits, inspections and approvals will reduce uncertainty, accelerate development, support businesses and create more jobs while maintaining strong standards.
explanations.capital_project_delays: Toronto needs stronger professional project management, transparent procurement and clear accountability. Major projects should have realistic budgets, schedules and performance targets, with regular public reporting to prevent delays and cost overruns.
explanations.capital_transparency: Major projects should be transparent. Residents deserve clear information on budgets, schedules, progress and performance to ensure accountability and responsible use of public funds.
explanations.construction_capacity: Toronto should expand skilled-trades training and apprenticeships while accelerating recognition of international credentials. A stronger, more inclusive construction workforce will help build housing and infrastructure faster and create good jobs.
explanations.cycling_network: Toronto should complete approved cycling projects while balancing cyclist safety with traffic flow, parking and local access. New lanes should be added where they are safe and practical, without unnecessarily increasing congestion.
explanations.encampment_removal: Safe, appropriate indoor housing should always come first. Once suitable accommodation is available, parks should remain safe, clean and accessible public spaces for everyone.
explanations.housing_as_of_right: Yes. Toronto should enable more housing, including well-designed mid-rise development, while respecting neighbourhood character, infrastructure capacity, green space and community needs.
explanations.housing_city_role: Toronto should streamline approvals, reduce construction barriers and enable more mid-rise and affordable housing, while partnering with non-profit and private-sector builders to deliver homes faster.
explanations.housing_cost_reduction: Faster, predictable approvals can reduce costs and accelerate housing delivery. Toronto should expand as-of-right zoning, automate routine permits and encourage well-designed mid-rise housing near transit while maintaining strong safety and design standards.
explanations.housing_density_location: Toronto should prioritize well-designed mid-rise housing along major streets and transit corridors, creating complete communities with homes, jobs, services and green spaces while reducing congestion.
explanations.housing_intervention: Toronto should accelerate housing approvals and reduce unnecessary costs. Faster permits can encourage mid-rise development, increase housing supply and help create more affordable homes in complete, sustainable communities.
explanations.infrastructure_backlog: Toronto should prioritize repairing and maintaining existing infrastructure before funding new expansion. Better asset management, efficient spending and responsible planning can reduce the backlog without placing new financial burdens on residents.
explanations.infrastructure_revenue: Toronto should improve transit and reduce congestion through smarter urban planning and better transportation infrastructure, rather than adding new financial burdens on residents.
explanations.performance_metric: Voters should judge my performance by measurable housing results: more homes approved, under construction and completed, with faster approvals and well-planned communities near transit.
explanations.police_budget: Toronto should maintain strong and effective policing while improving efficiency, accountability and community safety. Resources should focus on frontline officers, faster response times and prevention without creating unnecessary financial pressure on residents.
explanations.property_tax_growth: Property-tax revenues should grow responsibly with inflation and population, while the City improves efficiency, controls unnecessary spending and protects essential services.
explanations.protest_access: Peaceful protest must be protected, while clear rules should ensure access to hospitals, transit and essential services. Toronto can respect democratic rights while maintaining public safety and mobility.
explanations.provincial_approach: Toronto should work constructively with the Province to secure funding and faster approvals for housing, transit and infrastructure, while firmly advocating for Toronto’s priorities and long-term needs.
explanations.public_realm_priority: Toronto should prioritize clean, safe and well-maintained public spaces. Reliable roads, sidewalks, snow clearing, public washrooms and park maintenance are essential. Strong basic services should come first, while strategic improvements can follow.
explanations.revenue_source: Toronto should rely more on revenues generated by growth and real-estate activity, while encouraging responsible development and protecting residents from additional broad taxes and excessive user fees.
explanations.road_pricing: Toronto should improve transit and reduce congestion through smarter urban planning and better transportation infrastructure, rather than adding new financial burdens on residents.
explanations.safety_investment: Public safety requires prevention as well as enforcement. Toronto should strengthen mental-health response, addiction treatment and youth intervention, while ensuring police can focus their resources on serious crime and urgent public-safety threats.
explanations.service_delivery_model: Toronto should use competitive delivery where it provides better value, while maintaining strong public oversight. Contracts must include transparent costs, clear performance standards and accountability to ensure quality services and protect taxpayers.
explanations.street_space_priority: When street space is limited, priority should go to moving the greatest number of people safely and efficiently. Strong transit, walkable streets and cycling can reduce congestion while keeping Toronto accessible and connected.
explanations.strong_mayor_powers: Strong mayor powers should be used carefully and transparently, mainly to accelerate housing approvals and responsible development. They should help remove unnecessary delays while respecting good planning, infrastructure and community needs.
explanations.surveillance_tech: Toronto should use surveillance technology only under strict rules, with clear limits on data access, retention and sharing, independent audits, and strong privacy protections. Public safety must not come at the expense of residents’ rights.
explanations.technology_investment: Toronto should invest in smart, user-friendly digital services that make permits, licences, payments and service requests faster and easier, reducing delays and bureaucracy while improving accessibility and transparency for residents and businesses.
explanations.transit_funding_priority: Toronto should first make existing transit more frequent, reliable and efficient. Better service reduces waiting times, improves daily mobility and encourages more residents to choose public transit.
explanations.ward_commitment_target: Prioritize well-designed mid-rise housing near transit, with faster approvals and complete communities including green space, local services and infrastructure. This will increase housing supply while supporting livable neighbourhoods.
explanations.ward_objective: Prioritize housing growth through smart mid-rise development, faster approvals and investment near transit, while creating jobs and complete, sustainable communities.

answers.bio:
I believe Toronto deserves leadership that listens, takes action, and delivers results.

I immigrated to Canada from Ukraine in 2005, and I understand what it means to build a life through hard work, determination, and opportunity. I have dedicated my career to public service and to standing up for people when they need someone in their corner.

For over six years, I served our community through the Office of MPP Kinga Surma, helping thousands of residents navigate government, access housing and social supports, find employment opportunities, support their small businesses, and get the services they need.

As a Community Liaison with the Toronto Police Service, I work to strengthen relationships between residents, police, and community partners because I believe everyone deserves to feel safe in their neighbourhood.

My commitment to helping people extends beyond government. Since the outbreak of the war in Ukraine, I have helped displaced families navigate immigration, settlement, and employment opportunities. I am also actively involved with Yellow Brick House, supporting its work helping women and children escape domestic violence and rebuild their lives in safety.

In 2021, I ran for federal office because I believed government could—and should—do better.

Now, I am ready to bring my experience, determination, and commitment to City Hall—to make Toronto safer, more affordable, more accountable, and a city where families, seniors, newcomers, and businesses can thrive.

For me, public service isn’t about politics. It’s about people—and getting results.

explanations.arts_culture_support: Toronto should protect existing cultural venues, performance spaces and creative workspaces from displacement. Smart planning and property measures can preserve the places that give our neighbourhoods character, support local artists and keep Toronto’s arts and nightlife vibrant.
explanations.av_conditions: Autonomous taxi services must serve all Torontonians, not just the most profitable areas. Toronto should require strong accessibility, citywide coverage and minimum service standards to ensure seniors, people with disabilities and residents across the city have reliable access.
explanations.budget_gap_first: Toronto should first reduce unnecessary administrative, staffing and contract costs before asking residents to pay more. The City must review spending, eliminate duplication and inefficiencies, and ensure taxpayers receive the best possible value from every dollar.
explanations.business_attraction: Toronto must get the fundamentals right: affordable housing, reliable transportation, safe streets and a high quality of life. When people want to live and work here, employers, investment and major events will follow—creating jobs and strengthening our economy.
explanations.business_climate: Toronto must accelerate permits, inspections and approvals by cutting unnecessary red tape and modernizing City processes. Faster approvals will lower costs, attract investment, help businesses grow, create more jobs for residents and make Toronto more competitive.
explanations.capital_project_delays: Once a project is approved, its scope should not be changed without clear justification and identified funding. Toronto needs stronger accountability to prevent political changes from driving delays and cost overruns, while ensuring projects are delivered on time and on budget.
explanations.capital_transparency: Absolutely. Toronto residents deserve full transparency and accountability from their City. Major capital projects should have publicly available budgets, timelines and performance updates so residents can see how their tax dollars are being spent.
explanations.construction_capacity: Toronto should partner with skilled-trade unions such as LiUNA Local 183 to expand apprenticeships and training, while improving recognition of international credentials. Building our skilled workforce will create jobs and help deliver housing and infrastructure faster.
explanations.cycling_network: Review and redesign bike lanes that worsen safety or congestion or have low ridership. Where practical, move cycling routes to safer secondary roads and laneways, protecting cyclists while keeping major arterial roads moving for transit, emergency vehicles and traffic.
explanations.encampment_removal: Yes. If appropriate indoor space is available and meets a person’s accessibility, safety and household needs, they should be required to leave the encampment. Our parks must remain safe, clean and accessible to everyone.
explanations.housing_as_of_right: It depends on the size and scale of the dwelling. I support allowing more housing as-of-right where new development remains consistent with the existing height and character of the neighbourhood. Toronto does not have enough rental housing but we need to ensure that new development fits communities.
explanations.housing_city_role: By bringing together government resources and outside expertise, we can build affordable and supportive housing faster and more efficiently. At the same time, the City must set clear affordability requirements, monitor results and ensure taxpayers receive value for every public dollar invested.
explanations.housing_cost_reduction: Toronto should expand appropriate as-of-right zoning, automate routine permits and cut unnecessary delays. Time is money—reducing red tape and approval times will lower construction costs and help get much-needed housing built faster.
explanations.housing_density_location: These areas are best positioned to accommodate growth because residents have better access to transportation, services and employment. We should increase housing supply while ensuring that growth is supported by the infrastructure and community services needed to maintain quality of life.
explanations.housing_intervention: We need housing that people can actually afford, while providing appropriate supports for those experiencing homelessness so they can move into stable, permanent homes.
explanations.infrastructure_backlog: Toronto should review its assets and identify underused or costly facilities that are no longer sustainable. Selling or consolidating these properties can reduce long-term maintenance costs and redirect resources toward essential infrastructure, while protecting important community services.
explanations.infrastructure_revenue: No. Toronto residents already pay significant property taxes. We should work with other levels of government to address our infrastructure needs while conducting a thorough review of the City’s budget to find efficiencies, improve accountability, and ensure long-term sustainability.
explanations.performance_metric: Safer, cleaner and better-maintained streets and public spaces. Residents should be able to see and feel the difference in their neighbourhood. I want to be judged on whether our community is safer, cleaner and better managed, while delivering these improvements responsibly with taxpayers’ money.
explanations.police_budget: As Toronto grows, our police service must have the staffing and resources needed to respond effectively, address violent and hate-motivated crime, improve community presence and keep our neighbourhoods and transit system safe.
explanations.property_tax_growth: Property-tax revenues should generally grow with inflation and population, not through excessive tax increases. Toronto must live within its means, find efficiencies and ensure residents receive better value for the taxes they already pay.
explanations.protest_access: Peaceful protest is a democratic right, but it must remain peaceful, free from hate speech, and not block major roads, transit, hospitals or essential services. Toronto must protect lawful expression while keeping our city safe, moving and accessible.
explanations.provincial_approach: Toronto must work collaboratively with the provincial government to secure funding and approvals for key priorities. By finding common ground on housing, transit and infrastructure, we can deliver better results for Toronto residents.
explanations.public_realm_priority: Basic maintenance should come first. Residents deserve clean streets, well-maintained roads and sidewalks, reliable snow clearing, accessible public washrooms and properly maintained parks. Getting the basics right is essential before we move to major improvements.
explanations.revenue_source: Toronto should prioritize growth and transaction-based revenues rather than placing additional pressure on homeowners through property-tax increases. As the city grows, development and real-estate activity should contribute fairly to the infrastructure and services that growth requires.
explanations.road_pricing: Before introducing new tolls or congestion charges, Toronto should reduce congestion by completing infrastructure projects on time, moving bike lanes off major arterial roads where appropriate, and strictly enforcing no-parking rules during peak hours.
explanations.safety_investment: Toronto needs a visible and effective police and bylaw presence to deter crime, respond to disorder and keep our public spaces safe. At the same time, enforcement should work alongside prevention, mental health supports and community partnerships to address problems before they escalate.
explanations.service_delivery_model: Toronto should use specialized agencies where they can deliver services more efficiently and effectively. Clear performance targets, professional expertise and strong accountability can reduce bureaucracy, improve results and ensure taxpayers receive better value.
explanations.street_space_priority: Our streets must allow emergency vehicles to respond quickly, people with accessibility needs to travel safely, and businesses and trades to operate efficiently. A functioning city depends on the reliable movement of people, goods and essential services.
explanations.strong_mayor_powers: Strong mayor powers should focus on administration—ensuring City Hall is effective, accountable and focused on results. The Mayor should be able to build a strong leadership team and restructure departments when necessary to improve services and deliver better value.
explanations.surveillance_tech: Technology such as automated licence-plate readers can be an important tool for public safety, but its use must be carefully regulated. Toronto should establish clear rules governing access, data retention and sharing, with strong privacy protections and regular audits to prevent misuse.
explanations.technology_investment: Toronto should invest in technology that makes City services faster and easier to access. Residents and businesses should be able to obtain permits and licences, make payments and track service requests through simple, reliable digital systems that reduce wait times and red tape.
explanations.transit_funding_priority: Toronto residents need more frequent, reliable and safe transit on the routes they already use every day. Before committing significant funding to new expansion, we must improve existing TTC service, reduce delays and overcrowding, and ensure riders can get where they need on time.
explanations.ward_commitment_target: By December 2029, reduce reported crime in Ward 12 by 25% through stronger enforcement and police visibility, while reducing congestion through better traffic flow, rush-hour parking enforcement and advancing an Allen Road redesign, including a roundabout.
explanations.ward_objective: Safety and order must be a priority. Residents deserve safe streets, parks, transit and public spaces. I will support effective enforcement, address crime and public disorder, and work with police, community partners and all levels of government to keep our neighbourhoods safe.

explanations.av_conditions: Toronto should prioritize mandatory data disclosure to ensure transparent reporting on trips, collisions, congestion, and curb use, while maintaining accessibility and service standards and avoiding unnecessary municipal conditions beyond provincial regulation.
explanations.budget_gap_first: When facing a structural budget gap, Toronto should first reduce or redesign lower‑priority services, cut internal administration, staffing, and contract costs, maximize revenue from its own assets, and only then consider taxes, fees, or new revenue measures.
explanations.business_attraction: Toronto should attract major employers by using targeted incentives where appropriate, strengthening citywide fundamentals like housing, transportation and safety, and focusing sector strategies on industries where the city already has a competitive advantage.
explanations.business_climate: Toronto should improve its business climate by lowering commercial costs, reducing delays in permits and inspections, and strengthening fundamentals such as housing, transportation, public safety, and infrastructure.
explanations.capital_project_delays: Reduce project delays and cost overruns through transparent, competitive procurement, engineering‑based evaluation, and strict accountability. Integrate financial planning across governments, eliminate duplication, simplify processes, reduce waste, and align spending with long‑term economic trends.
explanations.capital_transparency: YES - Publishing project‑level budgets, schedules, and performance metrics strengthens transparency, engineering‑based oversight, disciplined planning, and accountability across all major capital programs.
explanations.construction_capacity: Toronto should increase construction capacity by maintaining a predictable long‑term project pipeline, expanding workforce training and credential recognition, and improving productivity through modular construction, prefabrication, and more efficient building methods.
explanations.cycling_network:

explanations.encampment_removal: When an indoor space meets safety, accessibility, and household needs, transitioning supports coordinated services, reduces risk, and aligns with integrated public‑safety and health‑system standards.
explanations.housing_as_of_right: Citywide intensification can improve supply and reduce approval complexity, if supported by engineering‑based assessments of infrastructure capacity, safety, market impacts, and neighbourhood cohesion.
explanations.housing_city_role: Strengthen affordability through streamlined regulatory pathways, reduced inter‑agency duplication, and predictable approval timelines. explanations.housing_cost_reduction: Cost reduction in Toronto’s housing delivery should be achieved through simplified approvals, reduced duplication, predictable regulatory conditions, and integrated municipal‑provincial‑federal programs that lower administrative overhead.
explanations.housing_density_location: Focusing density on major corridors and transit nodes supports demand‑driven planning, optimizes existing infrastructure, improves mobility outcomes, and concentrates growth where engineering assessments show the strongest capacity and long‑term performance.
explanations.housing_intervention: Use engineering‑based planning to align housing with demand and lifecycle costs. Improve affordability through streamlined approvals and reduced duplication. Integrate related government programs to protect taxpayers’ single wallet.
explanations.infrastructure_backlog: The infrastructure repair backlog is an operational defect caused by inadequate planning and preventive maintenance. explanations.infrastructure_revenue: Infrastructure reliability requires disciplined engineering standards, lifecycle maintenance, and efficiency‑based savings. Revenue tools must PROTECT taxpayers’ single wallet and prevent costly deferral of essential repairs.
explanations.performance_metric: Reduced operating budget by 15% through efficiency gains, consolidation, and eliminating duplicated administration—not service cuts. Stabilized property taxes through waste reduction, simplified processes, and alignment with long‑term economic trends.
explanations.police_budget: Increase police presence and response reliability by reducing administrative burden and directing resources to frontline operations, supported by clear service accountability and streamlined processes.
explanations.property_tax_growth: Residential property tax should be REDUCED, with the shortfall offset through efficiency gains, integrated financial planning, transparent competitive procurement, engineering‑based evaluation, fewer duplicated administrative structures, and reduced city‑appointed directors — NOT service cuts.
explanations.protest_access: Protests must be properly planned, safely managed, and conducted peacefully, with clear controls that protect public order and uphold lawful expression.
explanations.provincial_approach: Taxpayers fund all governments, so partnership and coordination is essential to eliminate redundancy, protect the single wallet, align operations under unified priorities and long‑term planning, and ensure accountability, metrics, procurement discipline, and strict timelines.
explanations.public_realm_priority: Toronto should prioritize basic maintenance to ensure clean, safe and reliable public spaces, while balancing selective major improvements and programming that support activity, community use and economic vitality.
explanations.revenue_source: Rely on best‑and‑highest use of city assets and cost reduction—not new revenue—achieved through efficiency gains, integrated financial planning, transparent competitive procurement, consolidation, strict accountability, simplified processes and eliminating duplicated administration.
explanations.road_pricing: Road planning must follow engineering‑based demand analysis, evidence‑driven capital planning, lifecycle maintenance, and streamlined processes. explanations.safety_investment: Strengthen public safety, crisis prevention, public space management, neighbourhood cohesion, and community stability through coordinated prevention, enforcement, and integrated recovery‑focused supports delivered jointly across municipal, provincial, and federal partners.
explanations.service_delivery_model: Public employees deliver most municipal services more efficiently than contractors. Contractors are effective for short‑term heavy construction, but long‑term services are more reliable, secure, and cost‑effective when performed by municipal staff, particularly under strong, disciplined leadership.
explanations.street_space_priority: Prioritize congestion reduction by removing unnecessary restrictions, simplifying transit‑roadway interfaces, improving system efficiency through integrated operations, and planning future street capacity using demographic trends, user forecasts, and long‑term mobility needs.
explanations.strong_mayor_powers: Strong‑mayor authority should enforce simplification across ~120 agencies, intergovernmental coordination to eliminate redundant programs and protect taxpayers’  wallet, and decisions anchored in affordability, accountability, transparent metrics, public safety, and long‑term planning discipline.
explanations.surveillance_tech: Limit surveillance technology to targeted, high‑risk investigations and legally justified assessments, with deployment governed by strict rules for access, data retention, and data sharing.
explanations.technology_investment: Prioritize tech investment in resident services for faster permits and payments, internal operations to improve procurement and administrative efficiency, and performance systems that provide public data, measure outcomes, and strengthen departmental accountability.
explanations.transit_funding_priority: Transit funding must focus on reliability and measurable mobility performance through streamlined operations, engineering‑driven capital planning, and disciplined lifecycle maintenance.
explanations.ward_commitment_target: Toronto faces operational, financial and structural challenges affecting services, infrastructure, affordability and long‑term planning. Modern governance requires improved administration, evidence‑based planning, disciplined management, and tools essential for a modern public organization.
explanations.ward_objective: Investment, housing, and development must support growth and human needs, with engineering‑based long‑term planning aligned to demographic and market trends, affordability strengthened through simplified approvals, integrated programs, and social supports with performance standards.

I am a community-minded entrepreneur, advocate, and young Toronto resident running for City Councillor in Ward 12 – Toronto–St. Paul’s. At 25, I bring a new generation’s perspective to municipal politics, shaped by the everyday experience of working, studying, building a career, and living in Toronto.
Through my work in construction, business administration, and client relations, I have gained practical experience working with people from different backgrounds and understanding the challenges facing residents, families, and small businesses. My community involvement has reinforced my belief that effective leadership starts with listening, being accessible, and following through.
I am running because I believe Ward 12 deserves a strong, practical voice at City Hall, one focused on the issues that affect people’s daily lives: housing affordability, responsible development, reliable transit, infrastructure, neighbourhood services, and keeping Toronto livable for families, seniors, workers, and young people.
My approach is straightforward: listen first, work collaboratively, and focus on results rather than political labels. I believe municipal government should be accountable, responsive, and connected to the communities it serves.
My campaign is guided by a simple principle: Ward 12 raised me, and now it’s time to give back.
answers.ward_commitment_target: Complete at least 20 priority road, sidewalk, park, lighting and public-realm improvements across Ward 12 by December 2029.

explanations.arts_culture_support: Toronto should invest in arts, culture and nightlife because they contribute to our economy, identity and quality of life. Public funding, affordable cultural spaces and access to City facilities can help local artists and organizations thrive while keeping culture accessible to residents.
explanations.av_conditions: If autonomous taxis operate in Toronto, they should serve Toronto, not just the most profitable areas. The City should require accessibility, reasonable geographic coverage and minimum service standards so new technology improves mobility for residents across the city.
explanations.budget_gap_first: Toronto should first look for efficiencies within its own operations, including administration, staffing and contracts. Residents should not face higher taxes before the City has demonstrated that it is controlling costs, eliminating waste and delivering services as efficiently as possible.
explanations.business_attraction: Toronto should compete by being a great place to live, work and invest. Reliable transit, attainable housing, safe and clean public spaces, and strong infrastructure are more sustainable than relying on costly incentives to attract employers, investment and major events.
explanations.business_climate: Toronto’s business climate depends on the fundamentals. We need reliable transportation, housing people can afford, safe and well maintained public spaces, and strong infrastructure. Businesses are more likely to invest and grow when the city is reliable and functional.
explanations.capital_project_delays: Toronto needs stronger project management and procurement from the start. Clear accountability, realistic timelines, competitive contracting and regular public reporting can reduce delays and overruns while ensuring major projects deliver the value taxpayers expect.
explanations.capital_transparency: Yes. Toronto residents deserve to know what major projects cost, whether they are on schedule, and how public money is being spent. Transparent, project-level reporting would strengthen accountability, identify problems earlier, and help rebuild public trust in City Hall.
explanations.construction_capacity: Toronto should embrace modern construction methods that reduce costs, shorten timelines and improve productivity. Modular construction, prefabrication and better technology can help us build more housing and infrastructure faster while maintaining strong safety and quality standards.
explanations.cycling_network: Toronto should complete the cycling projects already approved and evaluate their results before significantly expanding or removing road space. Future projects should be guided by safety, usage, accessibility and local transportation needs, with transparent performance data.
explanations.encampment_removal: When a safe, accessible indoor option genuinely meets a person’s needs, the City should require the encampment to be vacated. This must be paired with compassion, due process, and continued support to ensure people are not simply moved from one unsafe situation to another.
explanations.housing_as_of_right: I support more housing as-of-right across Toronto, including gentle density in areas dominated by detached and semi-detached homes. Growth must be matched with infrastructure, transit, parks and services so neighbourhoods can grow without overwhelming the communities already there.
explanations.housing_city_role: Toronto should take a stronger direct role in building and owning affordable and supportive housing. We cannot rely entirely on the private market to solve a public need. The City should also partner with non-profits and other levels of government to expand delivery.
explanations.housing_cost_reduction: Toronto should make it faster and more predictable to build housing by expanding as-of-right zoning and streamlining routine approvals. Reducing unnecessary delays lowers costs without sacrificing safety, quality, accessibility or appropriate community planning.
explanations.housing_density_location: Toronto should focus the greatest density along major streets and near rapid transit, while allowing gentle density across neighbourhoods. Growth should follow infrastructure capacity, with transit, roads, parks and community services planned alongside new housing, not after it.
explanations.housing_intervention: Toronto needs to build more housing that ordinary residents can actually afford. I would prioritize significantly expanding affordable and supportive housing, while also speeding approvals and allowing appropriate density so we increase supply across the city.
explanations.infrastructure_backlog: Toronto should fix what we already have before taking on more. I would prioritize maintaining roads, bridges, transit, water systems and public facilities before expanding the City’s asset base. New projects should proceed when they are properly funded and sustainable.
explanations.infrastructure_revenue: Yes, but new revenue must come with accountability. Toronto cannot keep deferring critical repairs. We should responsibly raise local revenue while demanding stronger support from other governments, prioritizing roads, bridges, transit, water infrastructure and other essential services.
explanations.performance_metric: I want voters to judge me on a measurable Ward 12 commitment that we set together. I would establish clear priorities with residents, publish progress publicly, and be accountable for delivering results not simply making promises during an election.
explanations.police_budget: Toronto needs effective policing, but every public dollar must deliver results. I would maintain the Police budget roughly in line with inflation while pushing for greater accountability, measurable outcomes, and stronger civilian services for issues better addressed outside policing.
explanations.property_tax_growth: Property taxes should generally keep pace with inflation and population growth to maintain essential services without placing an excessive burden on residents. The City must also find efficiencies, control spending, and pursue other sustainable revenue sources.
explanations.protest_access: The right to protest is fundamental, but it must be balanced with public safety and access to essential services. Clear, consistent rules should protect demonstrations while ensuring hospitals, transit, major roads and essential facilities remain accessible.
explanations.provincial_approach: Toronto and Ontario must work together. I would pursue a practical partnership that secures funding and delivers results for residents, while advocating firmly for Toronto’s needs. We should work with every level of government, regardless of political affiliation.
explanations.public_realm_priority: Toronto should get the basics right first. Clean streets, safe sidewalks, reliable snow clearing, well maintained parks and functioning public spaces directly affect residents every day. Before funding major beautification projects, we need to properly maintain what we already have.
explanations.revenue_source: Toronto needs predictable, sustainable revenue to fund essential services and infrastructure. I would prioritize broad recurring revenue over relying heavily on volatile real-estate activity or user fees, while ensuring lower-income residents are protected from disproportionate increases.
explanations.road_pricing: Yes, but only with clear accountability. Any road-pricing revenue must be dedicated to improving transit, reducing congestion and maintaining roads. Before introducing charges, the City should demonstrate that residents will see measurable improvements and that lower-income commuters are protected.
explanations.safety_investment: Public safety requires more than enforcement. We should invest in mental-health response, addiction treatment and youth programs that address problems before they become crises, while maintaining effective policing and bylaw enforcement when needed.
explanations.service_delivery_model: Toronto should use competitive contracting where outside providers can deliver better value, quality and accountability. This should never mean outsourcing for its own sake. The City should compare costs and outcomes and keep services in-house when that provides better long-term value.
explanations.street_space_priority: When space is limited, we should prioritize moving the greatest number of people safely and efficiently. Transit, walking and cycling should generally come first, while preserving essential access for deliveries, trades, emergency services and people with accessibility needs.
explanations.strong_mayor_powers: Strong mayor powers should be used sparingly but decisively when they can help address Toronto’s housing shortage. Used to advance housing and remove unnecessary barriers, while maintaining transparency, accountability and proper planning.
explanations.surveillance_tech: Surveillance technology can improve public safety, but it must not come at the expense of privacy. Toronto should establish strict rules for access, data retention, auditing and sharing, with clear oversight and consequences for misuse.
explanations.technology_investment: Toronto should invest in technology that makes government more transparent and accountable. Residents should be able to see how departments and major projects are performing, where money is being spent, and whether promised results are actually being delivered.
explanations.transit_funding_priority: Reliable transit comes first. Riders should not have to wait too long, deal with overcrowding or wonder whether their connection will arrive. I would prioritize improving frequency and reliability on existing routes while continuing long-term investment in expansion and maintenance.
explanations.ward_commitment_target: I will work with residents to identify the ward’s 20 highest-priority infrastructure and public-realm improvements, publish them publicly, and report progress annually. Voters should be able to see exactly what was promised, what was completed, and what remains outstanding.
explanations.ward_objective: Ward 12 needs growth, but growth must be matched by reliable core services. I would prioritize transit, road maintenance, parks, waste collection and local infrastructure so residents see tangible improvements in their daily lives while the ward continues to grow.

explanations.av_conditions: It is crucial for Toronto to have information on how autonomous taxi services are operating and the pitfalls involved in order to make policy that protects residents.
explanations.business_climate: Small business owners have made it clear to the campaign that operational expenses can be a burden for businesses who are given challenges such as tariffs. The City should do more to support small businesses including support for festivals and for cost-saving measures as identified by BIAs.
explanations.capital_project_delays: Too many projects in Toronto start and stagnate without additional construction due to a lack of funding. We must deliver on the projects that are promised, and they must be built expediently.
explanations.capital_transparency: It is crucial that the government has full transparency and honesty with the public, so that people are able to respond
explanations.cycling_network: There is great political uncertainty over bike lanes due to provincial decisions that has challenged the construction of cycling infrastructure on major streets.
explanations.encampment_removal: It is of the utmost importance to build trust and understand why a certain individual has chosen to not go to an available indoor space, and we must be mindful of these needs so that we are addressing the root issues as opposed to temporary, short-term solutions. The person at risk must cooperate.
explanations.housing_as_of_right: Toronto should permit more housing in every ward, but that development must happen responsibly and it should be ensured that we are building supportive & affordable housing across the city.
explanations.housing_city_role: All 3 of these roles must be taken on by the City of Toronto at different levels; The City Planning Department, The Housing Secretariat, and the Economic Development Unit can take on various responsibilities to advance the creation of affordable & supportive housing.
explanations.housing_cost_reduction: All 3 of these steps would have to be taken, as we need to not levy prohibitive taxes on those providing affordable housing. There needs to be responsible development, which means that while as-of-right zoning is positive, we must ensure new infrastructure is serving the communities it is in.
explanations.housing_density_location: For sustainable and equitable development, we must ensure that we are not concentrating growth in specific neighbourhoods, so that all of the various parts of the city are able to benefit from new development, and we can prevent displacement due to gentrification.
explanations.housing_intervention: There is a major need in Toronto for greater supply of affordable and supportive housing. Our current affordable housing waitlist is over 10 years long, and the city must meet the needs of its low-income, marginalized communities.
explanations.infrastructure_backlog: We should make sure that our current pipeline of projects has been completed before undertaking new ventures. It is crucial that we build equitably, on-time and under-budget so that residents can access the services they need.
explanations.infrastructure_revenue: We should not raise taxes at the municipal level, as it is the responsibility of the province and the federal government to ensure that municipalities are able to meet their infrastructure needs.
explanations.performance_metric: The ward commitment would be the expansion of affordable housing commitments specifically.
explanations.police_budget: De-tasking seems to be a proven method, and as more responsibilities are transferred away from TPS to civilian services such as Toronto Community Crisis Services, there needs to be a proportionate transfer of the budget accordingly.
explanations.property_tax_growth: By tying the increase in taxes with inflation & population, we can ensure there is a fair medium to raise property taxes that is in accordance with other significant factors. Other levels of government also have a responsibility to contribute to city funds.
explanations.protest_access: We want to ensure the right to protest is protected to the fullest extent possible while not worsening congestion on major streets. We should plan for and support road users.
explanations.provincial_approach: We should plan Toronto's budgets and services in a way where they can be suitably independent, without needing frequent assistance from other levels of government.
explanations.revenue_source: Property taxes currently makes up 30% of Toronto's annual revenue, and they are broadly consistent year-to-year. There is no need to implement new income or sales taxes, as the province could transfer a share of the existing income/sales taxes to the City instead.
explanations.road_pricing: In the midst of an affordability crisis, I'm opposed to all tolls and new taxes that make life difficult for residents of Toronto.
explanations.safety_investment: We have seen non-police interventions that emphasize crisis prevention and mental health be immensely successful. Toronto Community Crisis Response and other services require strong investments. We believe in prevention, not a cure as the solution to public safety.
explanations.service_delivery_model: We should build internal capacity, to ensure that we are not contracting out essential services to outside parties. It is crucial to maintain a strict line of accountability, where the City is answerable to deliver on city infrastructure.
explanations.street_space_priority: There has been a concerted push for pedestrianization in our downtown core, as residents are interested in connecting with their local streets. By prioritizing the needs of those taking public transit, walking or cycling, we are addressing the needs of the many residents who do not own vehicles.
explanations.strong_mayor_powers: City Council and other departments should be able to have a suitable amount of authority in their respective areas without concern on being overridden by the mayor. The principle of subsidiarity, where decisions are made at the most local level, is an essential one for a City like Toronto.
explanations.surveillance_tech: We want to ensure that the data is not abused and used for nefarious means, so we want to implement very strict rules over when and where it can be collected. Privacy is a paramount right for Torontonians, and they should feel secure from illegitimate surveillance.
explanations.technology_investment: Major investments in performance management is critically important so we can have an evidence-based approach to improve outcomes in all city departments.
explanations.transit_funding_priority: For large swathes of Torontonians, it is incredibly important that they are able to get to work, school or other commitments punctually. Many rely on the TTC to do so, whether that is through buses, streetcars or subways. This service must be as reliable and frequent as possible to meet those needs.
explanations.ward_objective: It is essential that we unlock the potential of new investment and development for our ward in a way that is responsible and beneficial for our communities. By tying social development with infrastructure investment, we can meet the needs of all residents equitably.

explanations.budget_gap_first: All three choices, they are not mutually exclusive.
explanations.housing_as_of_right: No more densification please.
explanations.housing_city_role: Six storey buildings on arterial roads only.
explanations.housing_density_location: Six storey buildings on arterial roads only.
explanations.housing_intervention: My real answer is none of the above, but we should reduce approval times for 6 storey projects on arterial roads which are the only types of projects I favour.
explanations.provincial_approach: We have to do all three, depending on the nature of the spend.
explanations.road_pricing: No to congestion charges (too much administration cost and hassle), but I would agree to raising parking lot fees and taxes to fund TTC improvements and expansion.
explanations.safety_investment: We can do all of them, they are not mutually exclusive.
explanations.street_space_priority: but exclude the curbside parking on arterial roads
explanations.technology_investment: Should be based on a ranked best value for investment dollar, so it could be on any one of the three choices.
explanations.transit_funding_priority: Really it's all of them, depending on the value provided.

answers.bio: Karina Lemke is a lifelong Torontonian, entrepreneur, and community advocate running for Ward 11 to bring back-to-basics leadership to Toronto City Hall. She believes that focusing on spending that produces results, community safety, stronger small business protections, neighbourhoods that work for everyone, harm prevention, and standing firmly against hate will restore trust in local government.

explanations.arts_culture_support: The City is about to destroy Chinatown, Little Italy, Portugal, Queen West. The plan to add transit priority on these streets will see the closure of 100s of cultural businesses. See: Little Jamaica. We cannot develop on top of what makes Toronto, Toronto.
explanations.av_conditions: None of these are my first choice. No autonomous taxi service has met regulatory standards, just peer reviews. Major red flag to jump to any of these.
explanations.budget_gap_first: If we agree there are too many layers of approval - there are too many people in those layers.
explanations.business_attraction: We have to win somewhere. But seriously, employers do not want to bring business to a drug den. Many factors are at play here.
explanations.business_climate: They of course are interconnected, but the battle to succeed as a small business keeps getting harder. SMEs account for ~50% of Canada's GDP.
explanations.capital_project_delays: There are so many empty buildings that could have kept rental businesses active for longer.
explanations.capital_transparency: Shockingly, many plans and budgets across City Hall do not have assigned goals.
explanations.construction_capacity: Tough again. But predictability allows management of the next two points.
explanations.cycling_network: Roads need to be planned as a grid. Currently, City Hall politicizes every part of every street. This isn't sustainable. In some areas, people who are not able-bodied are excluded from public life and public space. This is a human rights issue.
explanations.encampment_removal: Currently shelters are not meeting the needs of people who are unhoused. This issue is acute for women fleeing domestic violence, who cannot find safety in the current system.
explanations.housing_as_of_right: We have enough housing approved to last us beyond 2051.
explanations.housing_city_role: I recognize this is a build friendly survey, but not all developers are equally ethical, nor are they all good partners. Yes there are too many layers and restrictions (in some places), but a better working relationship that has a vision at the center need to be established for the good of Toronto.
explanations.housing_cost_reduction: These are all undesirable answers and only benefit developers. I selected the best of the worst.
explanations.housing_density_location: Tricky. Yes growth should occur near transit. Not the scale being permitted, and not based on a future idea of transit. Yes there should be low-rise/ multiplexes in neighbourhoods, not necessarily apartments. Creating rapid transit at the cost of culture will ruin this city.
explanations.infrastructure_backlog: I hope people are not answering that public land should be sold en masse to private dev. And I hope there isn't a plan to use the same (but repaired) infrastructure for more people.
explanations.infrastructure_revenue: Toronto is too dependent on developer money to solve all problems. This needs to be a better collaboration with government and developers so that decisions are the best, not the most desperate solutions.
explanations.performance_metric: This encompasses all answers really - If my goal is to have weekly street cleaning, that should be measured on maintenance, financial investment, performance.

answers.ward_commitment_target: I would complete 25 priority neighbourhood improvements in Davenport by December 2029, focused on pedestrian safety, streets, parks, lighting, cleanliness and transit-area improvements.

explanations.arts_culture_support: Make it easier for arts, culture and nightlife businesses to operate by simplifying permits, reducing unnecessary red tape and allowing flexible operating hours while maintaining reasonable safety and noise standards.
explanations.av_conditions: We should require autonomous taxi operators to provide Toronto with transparent data on trips, collisions, congestion, curb use and accessibility so the City can regulate based on evidence and protect the public interest.
explanations.budget_gap_first: Every department should demonstrate value for taxpayers. Reduce internal administration, staffing and contract costs first. Toronto should find efficiencies and eliminate unnecessary spending before cutting frontline services or increasing taxes and fees.
explanations.business_attraction: Toronto should compete by being a great place to live, work and invest. Our priority should be affordable housing, reliable transportation, public safety, efficient approvals and strong infrastructure—not expensive one-off incentives to attract individual companies or events.
explanations.business_climate: Toronto should make it faster and more predictable to open, expand and invest in a business. We should streamline permits, inspections and approvals, set clear service standards and hold City departments accountable when applications take too long.
explanations.capital_project_delays: Create a single, city-wide capital-project accountability system with one accountable project manager and mandatory change-order controls.
explanations.capital_transparency: Toronto should be transparent in its spending and accountability.  Toronto should be able to plan for additional costs ahead of time when planning projects.
explanations.construction_capacity: Toronto should expand apprenticeships, trades training and recognition of international credentials so we have the skilled workforce needed to build more housing and infrastructure faster.
explanations.cycling_network: Accelerate the expansion of safe, protected cycling routes, prioritizing connected networks and routes that improve safety and provide real transportation alternatives, while monitoring impacts on traffic, businesses and neighbourhoods.
explanations.encampment_removal: Choosing a safer option like housing is the best option for those that are de-housed. Parks are for everyone.
explanations.housing_as_of_right: Toronto needs to make good choices with ling term solutions to increase various types of housing along main roads where rapid transit is easily accessible.  Having a blanket ability to build housing within neighbourhoods can change the feel and character of areas unknowingly.  Plan things better.
explanations.housing_city_role: Some homes in Toronto along Main Street corridors were built in 1900-1930.  These homes should no longer occupy main street spaces.  Building better housing options along these thoroughfares is key.
explanations.housing_cost_reduction: Reductions in municipal development charges are necessary especially for projects that  deliver new housing. explanations.housing_density_location: Modifying housing within neighborhood’s will negatively affect the landscape of the home dynamics that makes Toronto great as well as loosing additional tax revenue.  Main transit corridor redevelopment is important.
explanations.housing_intervention: Main Roads that have the most public transit should be where Toronto focuses its efforts to build more housing including affordable housing.
explanations.infrastructure_backlog: Before asking residents for another dedicated levy, the City must demonstrate that it is managing its existing capital budget efficiently. explanations.infrastructure_revenue: Toronto should seek additional revenue streams that make sense and do not burden the people that live in the city.  We should also seek funding from other levels of government as we are an economic engine for Ontario
explanations.performance_metric: By the end of my term, Davenport will have a measurable improvement in the safety, cleanliness and condition of its streets and public spaces, with every major ward priority tracked publicly and progress reported to residents.
explanations.police_budget: The current police force is understaffed relative to our population, workload and service demands. With many veteran officers retiring there reds to be a larger budget to hire and train new officers to maintain thier current capabilities.

explanations.arts_culture_support: Entergagement Toronto™: make it easier to create markets, performances, nightlife, cultural events and experiences through simpler permits and sensible rules—while protecting safety and neighbourhoods.

explanations.business_climate: My Open for Business initiative means faster permits, inspections and approvals. Time is money for entrepreneurs. Toronto should make opening and growing a legitimate business easier—not become another obstacle.
explanations.capital_project_delays: Toronto OS means professional project management with public dashboards tracking budgets, schedules, change orders and outcomes. Identify overruns early—not after taxpayers receive the final bill.
explanations.capital_transparency: Absolutely. Every major project should have a public dashboard showing budget, timeline, delays, change orders and measurable progress. Taxpayers deserve receipts. As proposed in my Toronto OS! Transparency is Trust!
explanations.construction_capacity: Build Faster: encourage modular construction, prefabrication and modern building methods while Toronto OS modernizes approvals. We need to build more housing with less delay and greater productivity.

explanations.housing_cost_reduction: My Build Faster plan applies Toronto OS to permitting: automate routine pre-screening, run departmental reviews concurrently where possible and establish clear timelines. Less waiting means lower carrying costs and faster homes.
explanations.housing_density_location: Build density where mobility can support it: major corridors, rapid transit and appropriate commercial areas. Growth should be ambitious, infrastructure-aligned and well designed.

explanations.infrastructure_backlog: Fix what we own before building what we cannot maintain. Toronto OS would prioritize state-of-good-repair, rank projects by urgency and value, and avoid expanding the infrastructure backlog.

answers.bio:
Jason McDonald has spent 27 years cutting hair on Eglinton Avenue West. He owns Casual Beauty Salon at 1572 Eglinton Ave W — one of the few storefronts that survived the decade-long Crosstown LRT construction that shuttered more than 300 businesses in Little Jamaica.

He is the former Chair of the Little Jamaica BIA (York-Eglinton BIA) and became the public face of the fight for small-business compensation and community accountability during the transit build. He has appeared on CBC, CityNews, and CP24 and in the Toronto Star and NOW Toronto — not as a politician, but as a business owner who refused to let his community be erased quietly.

He is running for Toronto City Council in Ward 8 (Eglinton-Lawrence).

His platform is grounded in what he watched happen on Eglinton: development that serves the city's growth but too often leaves the surrounding neighbourhood behind. He supports building more housing, especially affordable units for households earning under $100,000, and believes Community Benefits Agreements must be negotiated with the community actually at the table — directing money toward the affordable housing, park improvements, flood protection, and small-business recovery the ward actually needs.

He is running because he believes Ward 8 can end the neglect it has endured for the last eight years — and that the people who built and held this community together through its hardest decade deserve a councillor who comes from the storefront, not the political class.

explanations.arts_culture_support: Little Jamaica waited 9 years for heritage protection. Preserve venues and cultural spaces before they're priced out.
explanations.av_conditions: Accessibility, geographic coverage and minimum standards — the whole city gets served, not just the profitable downtown core.
explanations.budget_gap_first: Cut the consultant and admin bloat first — the $58M consultant class — before touching services or raising taxes.
explanations.business_attraction: No more customized deals for the connected. Fix housing, transit and safety, and employers come because the city works — not because we bribed them.
explanations.business_climate: Delay is what killed 300 Eglinton businesses. Accelerate permits, inspections and approvals — speed is the cheapest business incentive.
explanations.capital_project_delays: The Crosstown was a procurement and project-management failure. Strengthen contracting, ban repeat offenders, and enforce what's actually in the contract.
explanations.construction_capacity: Recognize international credentials and expand apprenticeships — we have the people, they're locked out of the trades by paperwork.
explanations.cycling_network: Finish what's approved and measure it — but don't rip out parking and lanes on commercial streets where small businesses need deliveries.
explanations.encampment_removal: Parks belong to everyone — but a real offer must come with supports, not a sweep that leaves people with nowhere to go.
explanations.housing_as_of_right: More supply is essential — but it can't be blank-check upzoning. Density must deliver affordable units, parks and flood protection to the neighbourhood where it lands.
explanations.housing_city_role: City supplies land, funding and incentives to non-profit and private providers — and negotiates CBAs so the benefits land where the buildings go up.
explanations.housing_cost_reduction: Speed is the tax the city hides. Automate routine permits and expand as-of-right — with CBA and affordable-unit conditions attached, not stripped.
explanations.housing_density_location: Concentrate growth on Eglinton and near rapid transit, where density is supported — with CBA benefits staying in the corridor.
explanations.housing_intervention: Build and finance affordable and supportive housing for working families under $100K — funded through the commercial parking levy and development charges, not resident taxes.
explanations.infrastructure_backlog: Dedicated infrastructure levy from commercial sources, reserved exclusively for maintenance — not siphoned into consultant contracts or pet projects.
explanations.infrastructure_revenue: Yes. Deferring maintenance costs more later — the flood backlog west of the Allen proves it. But make corporations and developers pay, not homeowners.
explanations.police_budget: Hold the police budget roughly flat after inflation — and put new money into prevention, crisis response and lighting, not a bigger badge.
explanations.property_tax_growth: Residential property tax grows below inflation. New spending is funded by the commercial parking levy, billboard tax and fraud penalties — not the homeowner.
explanations.protest_access: Protest is protected — but with clear, published rules for locations, access routes and duration, so hospitals and small businesses can plan.
explanations.provincial_approach: Queen's Park writes cheques when it wants to. The city should plan on no new provincial money — and fund its priorities through the commercial parking levy and development charges.
explanations.public_realm_priority: Basics first — clean streets, clear sidewalks, working washrooms. The west end has waited long enough for routine care.
explanations.revenue_source: Commercial parking levy and development charges. Corporations and developers pay the costs their activities generate — not working families.
explanations.road_pricing: No. Fund transit through the commercial parking levy, billboard tax and development charges — not new tolls on working families
explanations.safety_investment: "The streets west of the Allen are darker, dirtier and less maintained than the east. Lighting, maintenance and active use fix safety before you need a badge."
explanations.service_delivery_model: Stop the $58M consultant churn. Rebuild permanent city capacity so the people doing the work answer to taxpayers, not a billing clock.
explanations.street_space_priority: Deliveries keep small businesses alive. Emergency vehicles keep people safe. Accessibility keeps everyone in. Essentials first — then we sort the rest.
explanations.strong_mayor_powers: If strong-mayor powers exist, deploy them for housing supply — with CBA and affordable-unit conditions attached, not stripped in the override.
explanations.surveillance_tech: Permit it with citywide rules — limits on access, retention, auditing and data sharing, so the watchers are watched too.
explanations.technology_investment: Public data and outcome metrics — so departments know they're being watched and taxpayers can see what their money bought.
explanations.transit_funding_priority: Concentrate growth on Eglinton and near rapid transit, where density is supported — with CBA benefits staying in the corridor.

answers.bio:
Like so many others in our community, I chose to live and work in Toronto Centre because it's the heart of Toronto and one of the most vibrant, welcoming, and inclusive places in the world.

For six years as your public school trustee, and the past four as your Councillor for Ward 13, I've been working to build a Toronto that's safe, liveable, affordable, and commutable.

As a former TDSB Trustee and Vice-Chair, I stood up for our schools, supported local families, and helped our children and communities reach their full potential.

As a former hospital healthcare worker and police officer, I've served on the frontlines, built deep roots here, and learned firsthand how to bring neighbourhoods, communities, and first responders together to improve safety while advancing equity and inclusion.

As a small business owner right here in Ward 13, I understand the challenges and the vital role local businesses play in keeping our neighbourhoods vibrant.

As a resident who has called Winchester Park, Cabbagetown South, Yorkville-Summerhill, and the Village home, I know how much we need better transit, smarter development, improved infrastructure, and revitalized services.

My story is our story. I'm working for all of us, and I'm dedicated to making our downtown better for everyone.

explanations.capital_project_delays: The City of Toronto doesn’t need to deliver every project itself, but it does need to have in-house expertise to learn from and improve delivery project-to-project, especially on major infrastructure initiatives which suffer from extraordinary cost inflation.
explanations.capital_transparency: We should always strive to be more accountable. This term, I passed a motion that requires staff to report all cost increases to projects under delegated authority. We should go a step further and require all project budgets and schedules to be published.
explanations.encampment_removal: In 2024 Council approved a human-rights based approach to the Encampment Protocol. City staff resolve encampments by building relationships and moving people safely indoors. We must keep working towards creating more effective and dignified transitional housing options.
explanations.housing_as_of_right: The way out of the housing crisis is to build every type of housing across the city. Building up, not out, will create more vibrant neighbourhoods and an equal distribution of services in every ward. That means multiplexes, midrise, and highrise buildings for Torontonians at all stages of life.
explanations.housing_city_role: All of the above, however I believe that the most efficient way for Toronto to deliver affordable housing is for Toronto to own affordable housing. Building new units, renovating existing stock, and converting existing underutilized units into public housing will add significantly to our portfolio.
explanations.housing_cost_reduction: Despite the creation of a national housing catalogue, Toronto has limited pre-approved designs for builders to use as-of-right. If properties meet specific dimensional and servicing criteria, there should be off-the-shelf housing options for immediate approvals.
explanations.housing_density_location: Every neighbourhood in Toronto needs to do its part in building housing. This will support a better diversity of housing types, bring families closer to undersubscribed schools and community facilities, and support ongoing and expanded service delivery.
explanations.housing_intervention: All of the above, but I chose public delivery because rapidly growing wards like Toronto Centre need more affordable and supportive public housing, delivered in partnership with not-for-profits, experienced builders, and other orders of government.
explanations.infrastructure_revenue: We should always do what we can as a city to address the backlog, as deferred work tends to result in even higher costs and risks major disruptions. Ontario is an outlier in how little infrastructure support is provided by the province and Toronto needs a new deal to meet the funding shortfall.
explanations.police_budget: Over the last term, increases have been made to the police budget to put TPS in a good position. Our 5-year hiring plan will recruit 360 new officers per year to help deliver on TPS’ mandate.
explanations.property_tax_growth: Toronto's lowest-in-Ontario property taxes mean underfunded services. Last Council, modest increases brought extended library hours, affordable housing, and more frontline staff. Aligning our rates with neighbouring cities fixes this at minimal cost to residents.
explanations.protest_access: The right to demonstrate and protest is integral to a free, democratic society. This must be curbed only carefully and proportionately to protect others' lives, safety, and rights.
explanations.revenue_source: Toronto needs a more direct stake in economic growth and success. A share of the HST would better reflect the city’s role as a major economic engine in Ontario and incentivize investments and supports for commerce that grow the tax base and support job creation.
explanations.road_pricing: I support road-pricing measures, especially as a way to raise funds for transportation improvements that make it easier for everyone to get around. So far, Doug Ford has been a constant obstacle any time Council has asked for new ways to address our fiscal needs.
explanations.safety_investment: Being proactive will always be better than reacting after a situation has reached a crisis. If we do not provide effective pathways for stabilization, treatment, and support to break cycles of crisis, we will simply perpetuate the status quo.
explanations.service_delivery_model: City staff must understand project delivery to properly work with delivery partners. This should go hand-in-hand with moving to making consistent, rolling investments in infrastructure to build institutional memory, control costs, and smooth delivery schedules.
explanations.street_space_priority: Focusing on transit and active transportation is a no-brainer. It will make commuting more affordable, increase accessibility in every part of our city, and help us achieve our climate goals all at the same time. It is also the most sensible allocation of space per person moved.
explanations.surveillance_tech: The City of Toronto needs to understand the complexities of surveillance technologies, how the data is used, and where it is stored, in order to responsibly deploy it.
explanations.transit_funding_priority: In order for transit to be the preferred method of transportation for all Torontonians we need to invest in service. Predictability will increase ridership and rider satisfaction. Platform-level doors and other investments should be part of this program.

answers.bio: Bridget Ogundipe, a thirty-year Ward 4 resident, believes city decisions must be shaped by the people who live that daily reality. Bringing collaborative leadership to City Hall, she is running for City Council to fight for our community, ensuring it is an affordable, safe, and vibrant ward.To deliver on this vision, Bridget’s top priority is tackling the affordability crisis by championing the public builder model, encouraging responsible development, expanding diverse housing options including the "missing middle," and views stable housing as the foundation for long-term stability. She will fight for our community by protecting tenants, supporting city initiatives such as banning surveillance pricing in groceries, ensuring infrastructure keeps pace with growth, pushing for a reliable, affordable TTC, and advocating for more efficient, safer road design. She strongly believes our thriving small businesses are the heartbeat of our main streets. By removing unnecessary municipal barriers, investing in arts and youth programming, and moving away from top-down decision-making, she will bridge the gap between City Hall and residents.Bridget has witnessed firsthand the power of community and persistence to overcome barriers. Her path spans from growing up in Regent Park in the 80s and 90s, moving to the Junction in 95, to co-founding an international NGO to navigate tight budgets and major systemic hurdles to build critical infrastructure alongside local residents in Haiti and Jamaica. Having learned early how a single opportunity can change a life, she also co-founded a local film school and a non-profit youth mentorship program closer to home.

Odessa Paloma Parker is a cultural journalist, award-winning stylist, educator and brand strategist based in Toronto. She has held positions as both the Fashion and Art Editor at The Globe and Mail Style Magazine, and in 2022, she founded Opaloma, a stylish cultural platform featuring stories from Toronto and beyond. She is a co-author of the first edition of Louis Vuitton's City Guide Toronto, and her journalistic expertise has been acknowledged by an Honourable Mention for the 2021 National Magazine Award for “Best Column”. Odessa was also in the innovative role of Head of Content for a trio of cannabis brands in the year leading up to adult-use legalization in Canada.

In addition to supporting artists through her professional and philanthropic work, Odessa is passionate about promoting local talent and businesses within the city she has called home her whole life. Its astonishing to me that we might run an election, as large parts of Canada are on fire, and not make climate action the most important issue for the city to tackle.  In fact, council punted a decision on building emissions standards until after the election.

Climate Action is not a technology problem, or a money problem, its a political problem, and it belongs in every election.

Eighteen years ago I decided to refocus my architectural firm on the problem of decarbonizing buildings.  I am proud to be the architect of the City’s first Net-Zero building, the Mount Dennis Childcare.  I am also proud of The Elmwood, a seniors non-profit housing project that is the first net-zero ready affordable housing project approved under CMHC’s Apartment Construction Loan Program.

Despite successes, we can’t meet our climate goals one building at a time. We need government to align their efforts with the private sector for maximum reductions.  For example, the city can play a vital role in finance renovations using CPACE to transfer repayment to property tax bills.  With efforts like this, I can see a viable, affordable path to decarbonization in 20 years, which will contribute to climate stabilization.

I also serve at the Chair of the Toronto 2030 District, a non-profit dedicated to promoting the most affordable and best solutions to decarbonizing the City of Toronto.
